questions.q: State the definition of the derivative of a function \( f \) at a point \( x = c \) using the limit of the difference quotient. Write the expressions for the left-hand derivative and right-hand derivative.
questions.a: The derivative is \( f'(c) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \). Left-hand derivative: \( f'_-(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \). Right-hand derivative: \( f'_+(c) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \). A wrong answer (e.g., writing \( \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \) without specifying \( h \to 0 \), or confusing left/right limits) shows the student hasn't internalised the precise limit definition and the role of \( h \) approaching 0 from both sides.

questions.q: Explain why the existence of \( \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{f(c+h)-f(c)}{h} \) forces \( \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c) \). Use the identity \( f(x)-f(c) = \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \cdot (x-c) \) in your reasoning.
questions.a: If \( f'(c) \) exists, then \( \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} = f'(c) \) (finite). Then \( \lim_{x \to c} [f(x)-f(c)] = \lim_{x \to c} \left[ \frac{f(x)-f(c)}{x-c} \cdot (x-c) \right] = f'(c) \cdot 0 = 0 \), so \( \lim_{x \to c} f(x) = f(c) \). A wrong answer (e.g., "because derivative exists" without the product-of-limits step) reveals the student doesn't see the algebraic link between the difference quotient and the continuity condition.

questions.q: Check whether the function \( f(x) = \begin{cases} x^2, & x \le 1 \\ 2x-1, & x > 1 \end{cases} \) is differentiable at \( x = 1 \). Compute both one-sided derivatives explicitly.
questions.a:
Left-hand derivative: \( f'_-(1) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{(1+h)^2 - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{1+2h+h^2-1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} (2+h) = 2 \).
Right-hand derivative: \( f'_+(1) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{2(1+h)-1 - 1}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{2+2h-2}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^+} 2 = 2 \).
Both equal 2, so \( f \) is differentiable at \( x=1 \) with \( f'(1)=2 \). A common error is using the wrong piece for the limit (e.g., using \( x^2 \) for the right-hand limit) or forgetting to subtract \( f(1)=1 \) correctly.

questions.q: The function \( f(x) = |x-2| \) is continuous at \( x=2 \) but not differentiable there. Identify the left-hand and right-hand derivatives at \( x=2 \) and explain why they differ. Then sketch the graph near \( x=2 \) and describe the geometric feature that causes non-differentiability.
questions.a:
For \( x<2 \), \( f(x)=2-x \); for \( x>2 \), \( f(x)=x-2 \). At \( x=2 \), \( f(2)=0 \).
\( f'_-(2) = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{|2+h-2|-0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0^-} \frac{-h}{h} = -1 \).
\( f'_+(2) = \lim_{h \to 0^+} \frac{h}{h} = 1 \).
Since \( -1 \ne 1 \), \( f \) is not differentiable at 2. The graph has a sharp corner (cusp) at \( (2,0) \) — the tangent from the left has slope -1, from the right slope 1. A wrong answer that claims the derivative is 0 or doesn't compute both sides shows the student doesn't connect the absolute value's piecewise definition to the one-sided limits.

questions.q: A student argues: "The function \( f(x) = x^{1/3} \) is continuous at \( x=0 \), so it must be differentiable there." Evaluate this claim. Compute \( f'(0) \) using the definition and state whether the derivative exists as a finite number.
questions.a: \( f'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h^{1/3} - 0}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{1}{h^{2/3}} = +\infty \). The limit is not finite, so \( f \) is not differentiable at 0. The student's claim is false: continuity is necessary but not sufficient for differentiability. This counterexample shows a vertical tangent (infinite slope). A wrong answer that says "derivative is 0" or "derivative exists because function is continuous" reveals the misconception that continuity implies differentiability, and/or an algebraic error in simplifying \( h^{1/3}/h \).

questions.q: Construct a function that is continuous at \( x=0 \) but not differentiable at \( x=0 \), different from \( |x| \) and \( x^{1/3} \). Define it piecewise, verify continuity, and show the one-sided derivatives are unequal (or infinite).
questions.a:
Example: \( f(x) = \begin{cases} x \sin(1/x), & x \ne 0 \\ 0, & x = 0 \end{cases} \).
Continuity: \( |x \sin(1/x)| \le |x| \to 0 \), so \( \lim_{x \to 0} f(x) = 0 = f(0) \).
Derivative at 0: \( f'(0) = \lim_{h \to 0} \frac{h \sin(1/h)}{h} = \lim_{h \to 0} \sin(1/h) \), which does not exist (oscillates between -1 and 1).
Thus \( f \) is continuous but not differentiable at 0. A poor answer might give a function that isn't continuous, or one where the derivative exists, showing the student cannot design a counterexample that satisfies the precise conditions.
